Empirical scope is stronger than many interactive-system papers: three tool families, two datasets with distinct characteristics, 33 participants, 30 coding sessions, and both automatic metrics and interviews.

Appendices provide codebooks, prompts, operation details, dataset analyses, and a public release is claimed, supporting partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The causal claim about synchronous vs. asynchronous collaboration is weakened by the protocol: synchronous conditions use groups of three, while asynchronous conditions appear to be single coders with no consolidation. This confounds modality with labor, discussion, and group size.

The LLM condition is not a strong representative of current LLM-assisted coding: agreement is low in several settings, many outputs are unlabeled, and some codebooks for relational and LLM conditions appear nearly identical, which should be clarified.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored question: how collaboration modality affects NLP-assisted qualitative coding, a realistic workflow issue for human-in-the-loop NLP systems.
The study is broader than many prior evaluations, covering three system paradigms, two datasets, multiple evaluation dimensions, and a small user-study component.
The appendices provide useful artifacts such as final codebooks, LLM prompts, dataset statistics, and example alignment visualizations; the claimed public release would help reproducibility.
The correctness audit with multiple annotators is a valuable attempt to move beyond purely embedding-based or overlap-based measures.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not well isolated. Synchronous coding compares groups of three working together against individual asynchronous coders, without an asynchronous consolidation phase, so the study confounds modality with number of people, discussion/consensus, labor, and aggregation strategy.

The experimental design is badly underpowered at the level that matters: only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per condition, with repeated participants and a fixed order where repeated participants always did asynchronous first. Learning, expertise, assignment, and group-composition effects are not convincingly controlled.

The statistical analysis is not reliable enough to support the strength of the claims. Many t-tests are run without multiple-comparison correction, and the effective units appear to be themes or document pairs nested within the same few codebooks rather than independent experimental replicates, creating a serious risk of pseudoreplication.

Several evaluation metrics are questionable. Best-match Jaccard can inflate consistency by allowing many-to-one alignments and ignoring unmatched themes or theme-count differences; centroid similarities are nearly saturated and weakly discriminative; cohesiveness/distinctiveness from embeddings may reward semantic broadness rather than coding quality.

Correctness results are mixed and sometimes contradict the narrative: for example, synchronous relational coding is least accurate on climate ads, while asynchronous topic modeling is more accurate on COVID. The paper still draws broad recommendations favoring synchronous collaboration without adequately reconciling these tradeoffs.

The LLM condition is weakly specified and arguably not representative: the selected 3B model has low human-model agreement in several sessions, produces unlabeled documents, uses prompts that still refer to tweets even for ads, and offers much less user control than the other systems, making cross-system conclusions hard to interpret.

Dataset effects are discussed post hoc but remain confounded with many variables, including corpus size, document length, available auxiliary concepts, proportion of documents inspected, and domain. Some reported dataset statistics are also internally inconsistent, such as the Table 10 row labeled similarity > 0.3 despite the surrounding text describing values below 0.3.

The user study is too thin to support the design recommendations: the paper does not report a systematic qualitative analysis procedure, participant counts per interview condition, coding scheme, or enough evidence from interviews.

Reproducibility is only partial. Code and results are said to be public, but reproducing the human-interaction data, training protocol, time budgets, randomization, participant assignment, and statistical tests would require substantially more detail.

The empirical scope is ambitious, covering three tool families, two datasets with different properties, synchronous/asynchronous settings, and a post-hoc manual correctness evaluation.

The proposed multi-dimensional evaluation framing around consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness is useful and could help standardize evaluation of interactive qualitative-coding systems.
Reproducibility is helped by the public repository claim and by appendices listing prompts, codebooks, tool operations, dataset statistics, and theme counts.
weaknesses: The central causal claims about synchronous vs. asynchronous collaboration are not fully supported. There are only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system/dataset condition, some participants appear in multiple experiments, and randomization/counterbalancing and per-condition expertise balance are not sufficiently specified.

The statistical analysis is a major concern. Two-sample unpaired t-tests over theme- or document-derived quantities likely treat nested/dependent observations as independent, despite the true independent units being coding sessions/groups. Multiple comparisons, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and mixed-effects or permutation analyses are missing.

Several metrics have uncertain construct validity for qualitative-analysis quality. SBERT centroid/group-average similarities can be insensitive, best-match Jaccard does not enforce one-to-one alignment, the top-25% heuristic is ad hoc, and assignment correctness does not measure codebook completeness, interpretability, or usefulness to downstream qualitative inquiry.

The user study is underreported: the number of interviewees, coding/analysis procedure for interview responses, and links between qualitative claims and evidence are unclear, making the recommendations less rigorous than the quantitative sections.

The LLM condition is comparatively weak and potentially confounded: it uses a small Llama 3.2 3B model, low human-model agreement in several settings, prompt-selection details that may tune on human labels, and many unlabeled outputs. This limits conclusions about LLM-based interactive systems broadly.

The paper is clear overall, but some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, especially statements that results “strongly suggest” benefits of synchronous collaboration. The limitations section acknowledges scope but not the deeper statistical-independence and construct-validity issues.

strengths: The topic is relevant and timely: evaluation of NLP-assisted qualitative coding under realistic collaborative workflows is important for CL/NLP systems used in social science and HCI-adjacent analysis.

The paper studies three distinct families of interactive systems, two substantially different datasets, and both synchronous and asynchronous settings, giving the work broader empirical coverage than a single-tool case study.

The proposed dimensions of consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness are sensible starting points, and the paper usefully combines automatic embedding-based metrics with post-hoc human validation and participant interviews.
Reproducibility is partially supported through public code/data, reported hyperparameters, prompt templates, codebooks, and appendix details.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that collaboration modality affects output quality is not fully supported because modality is confounded with team size and process: synchronous runs use three coders jointly, while asynchronous runs appear to be single coders without the consolidation step typical of collaborative qualitative analysis.

The statistical analysis is weak for the study design. There are only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per cell, participants are reused, and theme/document-level comparisons are likely treated as independent in t-tests. This risks pseudo-replication and inflated significance; hierarchical, permutation, or bootstrap analyses would be more appropriate.

Several metrics have validity concerns. Maximum best-theme matching can ignore unmatched or extra themes and may inflate consistency; centroid similarities are often near ceiling and weakly discriminative; embedding-based cohesiveness is partly circular for systems that already use embeddings to partition or assign data.

Correctness evaluation is under-specified and not clearly tied to the inherently inductive nature of themes. The paper does not fully explain the rating rubric, blinding, how F1 is computed from pair judgments, or uncertainty around correctness estimates, and inter-annotator agreement is only moderate.

The comparisons across systems are confounded by different affordances and non-equivalent setup choices, such as using a query-driven topic model without queries, auxiliary concept labels in the relational system, and a small Llama 3.2 3B model with low human-model agreement and unlabeled outputs.

The user study is too lightly reported to substantiate design recommendations: interview sample size, analysis procedure, coding method, and saturation/triangulation are not described, and group versus individual interviews introduce another modality confound.

Some claims overreach the evidence, especially statements that synchronous collaboration enables deeper analysis or significantly improves quality, when results are mixed across datasets, systems, and correctness measurements and no multiple-comparison correction is discussed.

Clarity is generally good, but there are presentation and consistency issues, including typos, hard-to-read tables, missing uncertainty for Figure 4, and an apparent inconsistency in Table 10 about the percentage of pairs with similarity greater than versus less than 0.3.

The empirical scope is broader than many prior tool-specific evaluations, covering three different system families and two datasets with contrasting properties.

The proposed evaluation dimensions—consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness—are useful and help separate different notions of output quality rather than relying on a single agreement score.

The paper is generally clear, and the release of code and experimental outputs improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central causal claim about synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration is only weakly supported. The asynchronous condition appears to be individual coding without consolidation, while the synchronous condition uses three-person groups, so modality is confounded with group size, discussion, and labor allocation.

The number of independent experimental units is very small: only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per tool/dataset condition, with some participant reuse. This makes the reported statistical comparisons fragile.

The use of two-sample t-tests over theme/document-derived measurements likely involves pseudo-replication, since themes and documents within the same codebook are not independent experimental units. The significance markings therefore overstate evidential strength.

Several evaluation metrics depend heavily on SBERT embedding geometry and dataset-level homogeneity, so higher similarity may reflect corpus structure or broader labels rather than better qualitative themes. The validity of these metrics for qualitative analysis quality needs stronger justification.

The comparison across systems is not fully controlled: the topic model is run without input queries, the relational system uses auxiliary concepts, and the LLM setup uses a small 3B model with low human-model agreement and nontrivial unlabeled outputs. These differences limit conclusions about system families.

The correctness evaluation is promising but underdescribed: it is unclear how annotators judged correctness for subjective, coder-created themes, how F1 was computed from pair judgments, and whether annotators were blind to system or condition.

Some conclusions are stronger than the evidence warrants, especially claims that synchronous collaboration facilitates deeper analysis or that dataset characteristics determine when async/sync coding is preferable.
If submitted to a double-blind venue, the manuscript appears not to be anonymized, including author names, arXiv metadata, and a public repository link.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-evaluated problem for NLP-assisted qualitative analysis: how interactive theme discovery systems behave under realistic collaborative workflows rather than only isolated tool evaluations.

The empirical scope is substantial for a human-centered NLP study: three different system paradigms, two corpora with contrasting properties, 33 participants, 30 coding sessions, and a post-hoc manual assessment of 2,400 document-theme assignments.

The proposed evaluation dimensions, consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness, are a useful attempt to separate different notions of codebook quality, and the paper generally avoids claiming that a single collaboration mode or system is uniformly best.

The appendices provide useful operational details, final codebooks, LLM prompts, dataset diagnostics, and the authors state that code and experimental outputs are publicly available, which improves reproducibility relative to many user-study papers.
The combination of quantitative results with participant interviews gives the work practical relevance for the design of interactive NLP tools for qualitative researchers.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is weakened by the study design: synchronous groups contain three coders deliberating jointly, whereas asynchronous conditions are individual coders without a true asynchronous consolidation phase. Thus the comparison conflates modality, group size, deliberation, and consolidation strategy.

The number of independent experimental units is very small, with only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system-dataset setting. The reported unpaired t-tests appear to treat derived theme/document metrics as independent observations, which risks pseudoreplication and makes the statistical significance claims unreliable without a clearer hierarchical or mixed-effects analysis.

The quality metrics only partially validate qualitative-codebook quality. Best-match Jaccard/embedding alignment can hide split/merge errors and unmatched themes; SBERT-based cohesiveness is partly circular for systems using SBERT; very high centroid similarities suggest limited discriminative value; and theme counts vary substantially across runs.

The correctness evaluation is valuable but underspecified and somewhat subjective for inductive themes: there is no external gold standard, the definition of F1 is not fully clear from the main text, uncertainty is not reported, and agreement is only moderate. The empirical design is ambitious in scope, covering three families of interactive systems, two distinct datasets, quantitative metrics, manual assignment checks, and participant interviews.

weaknesses: The central comparison is badly confounded: asynchronous means single coders working alone, while synchronous means groups of three producing one codebook. This tests group size, consensus, labor, and interaction all at once, not collaboration modality alone; moreover, there is no asynchronous consolidation stage despite that being a standard workflow.

The statistical evidence is not reliable. There are only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per tool/dataset condition, yet the paper reports t-tests and significance over theme/document-derived quantities that are not independent. The proposed metrics have weak construct validity. Maximum best-match Jaccard or centroid alignment can map many themes to the same counterpart and does not penalize missing/extra themes or different granularity. SBERT centroid similarities are often near saturation, so they may not meaningfully distinguish codebook quality.

The correctness analysis is under-specified and only partially convincing. There is no external gold codebook, the figure lacks raw values/error bars, the claimed significant differences are not backed by tests, and moderate annotator agreement does not fully validate judging arbitrary participant-generated themes as correct or incorrect.

Dataset and system effects are heavily entangled. COVID and climate data differ in size, domain, length, formulaicity, and available auxiliary labels, so the paper cannot isolate which dataset properties drive the observed differences. Tool comparisons are also confounded by very different interfaces and intervention affordances.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-studied issue for NLP-assisted qualitative analysis: how collaboration setting, tool design, and dataset characteristics jointly affect coding outcomes.

The empirical scope is broader than many prior evaluations, covering three different interactive-system paradigms, two datasets with different properties, 33 participants, 30 sessions, automatic quality metrics, post-hoc correctness annotation, and interviews.

The evaluation is usefully multi-dimensional: consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness capture different failure modes, and the paper avoids claiming one universally best system or setting.
The paper appears reasonably reproducible in intent, with a public repository, appendices for prompts/codebooks/settings, and reporting of participant protocol and LLM compute details.
weaknesses: The central causal claim about synchronous vs. asynchronous collaboration is not fully supported. Synchronous sessions use groups of three while asynchronous sessions are individual and apparently not consolidated, so collaboration modality is confounded with group size, deliberation, and codebook-consolidation strategy.

The statistical analysis is a major concern. There are only 2 synchronous and 3 asynchronous independent sessions per dataset-system cell, but significance appears to be tested over derived theme/document similarities, which are nested and non-independent. The many t-tests and borderline p-value markings further weaken confidence.

Several metrics are only indirect proxies for codebook quality. Best-match Jaccard can inflate alignment, centroid similarity is nearly saturated in many settings, and SBERT intra/inter-theme similarity may reflect corpus geometry or system assignment behavior rather than human analytic quality.

The correctness evaluation is valuable but underspecified: 2,400 document-theme pairs is modest relative to the generated label space, agreement is only moderate, and it is unclear how blind annotators were to systems/settings or how subjective theme validity was handled.

The LLM condition is not well controlled or clearly comparable to the other systems. Human-model agreement is often low, many outputs are unlabeled, the 3B model may underrepresent current LLM capabilities, and the appendix shows suspiciously identical or highly overlapping codebooks between the relational and LLM conditions in some cases.

The paper sometimes overstates findings, e.g. claiming that results strongly suggest synchronous collaboration yields clearer themes, despite mixed correctness results and weak independence assumptions.
Presentation is generally understandable but has rough edges: dense tables, awkward formatting, typos, and some prompt templates that appear mismatched to the task reduce clarity and confidence.

The study compares three different classes of systems, two datasets with different properties, and multiple quality dimensions, giving the paper a broader empirical scope than many single-tool evaluations.
The authors make an effort to triangulate evidence using consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, post-hoc correctness judgments, and participant interviews rather than relying on one metric alone.
Reproducibility is helped by the stated public release of code/results and by reasonably detailed appendices for prompts, tool operations, datasets, and final codebooks.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that collaboration setting affects output quality is not convincingly supported. There are only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system/dataset condition, and repeated participants introduce additional dependence; this is far too little independent experimental replication for the strength of the paper's conclusions.

The statistical testing appears inappropriate or at least insufficiently justified. Theme-level or document-pair-level quantities are treated as if they were independent samples, despite being nested within very few codebooks and produced by the same systems/coders. Reported significance therefore gives a misleading sense of confidence.

Several major confounds are not controlled: participant expertise, repeated participation, group composition, time-on-task, different initial partitions/topic counts, different intervention affordances across systems, and different consolidation assumptions for asynchronous coding. These make it difficult to attribute observed differences specifically to synchronous vs. asynchronous collaboration.

The proposed metrics are only partially validated. Embedding-based cohesiveness/distinctiveness may reflect SBERT geometry and system assignment behavior rather than human-perceived theme quality, and best-match Jaccard/centroid alignment can hide unmatched or overgeneralized themes.

The correctness evaluation is underexplained. The figure reports F1 scores, but the paper does not clearly define how F1 is computed from sampled document-theme judgments, and key numeric results and significance analyses are missing from the text/table presentation.

strengths: The paper studies an important and underexplored problem: how collaboration modality affects NLP-assisted qualitative coding outcomes. This is relevant to CL/NLP because many proposed interactive analysis tools are evaluated in isolation and without realistic collaborative workflows.

The empirical scope is appreciable: three different classes of interactive systems, two datasets with contrasting properties, 30 coding sessions, post-hoc correctness checks, and participant interviews. This gives the work more substance than a purely conceptual evaluation proposal.

The paper makes a useful attempt to separate multiple notions of output quality, including consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness, rather than relying on a single agreement metric.

The appendices provide many operational details, prompt templates, final codebooks, dataset statistics, and the authors state that code and experimental data are publicly available, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that collaboration modality affects coding quality is only partially supported because the design confounds modality with group size and consensus process: asynchronous results are individual codebooks, while synchronous results are produced by three-person groups. The study also does not evaluate realistic asynchronous consolidation, despite that being a common qualitative workflow.

The statistical analysis is a major concern. There appear to be very few independent experimental units per condition, yet the paper reports many two-sample t-tests over derived theme/document metrics, highlights near-significance, and does not address pseudoreplication, normality, dependence among themes/documents, or multiple comparisons. This makes the significance markings and several strong claims unreliable.

Participant reuse and ordering introduce further confounds. Some participants appear in multiple experiments and always perform asynchronous sessions before synchronous ones, which may introduce learning, tool familiarity, or dataset familiarity effects.

Several metrics are reasonable descriptive probes but are overinterpreted as quality measures. SBERT centroid similarities are often near saturation, cohesion/distinctiveness depend heavily on embedding geometry and dataset homogeneity, and high semantic similarity does not necessarily imply a better qualitative codebook.

The LLM condition is comparatively weak and somewhat ad hoc: it uses a small Llama 3.2 3B model, prompt selection by agreement on human-labeled examples, and prompts that include odd wording such as code/object terminology. The model also produces nontrivial unlabeled rates, raising questions about comparability with the other systems.

The correctness evaluation is valuable, but important details are missing or underdeveloped: annotation guidelines, sampling per theme when theme sizes differ, adjudication procedure, and how correctness is defined for inherently interpretive qualitative themes. Moderate agreement is encouraging but not enough to fully validate the measure.

The dataset analysis contains some internal inconsistencies and overclaims. For example, the text describes climate ads as having more pairs below 0.3 similarity, while the corresponding table labels the percentage as greater than 0.3; the discussion of GMM confidence versus very low silhouette scores is also not well reconciled.

The paper would be much stronger if it framed the results as exploratory/descriptive evidence, reanalyzed the statistics at the correct unit of independence, reduced unsupported claims of significance, and more explicitly separated tool effects, dataset effects, participant effects, and collaboration effects.

strengths: The paper studies an important and underexplored problem: how collaboration modality affects NLP-assisted qualitative coding, a realistic setting for human-in-the-loop NLP systems.
The empirical scope is meaningful, covering three different system families, two datasets with different properties, 30 coding sessions, and both quantitative metrics and participant interviews.

The proposed evaluation dimensions, consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness, are sensible starting points and the paper makes a useful attempt to move beyond ad hoc evaluation of individual tools.

The appendices provide substantial operational detail, final codebooks, prompt templates, dataset analyses, and the paper states that code and experimental outputs are publicly available, supporting partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central comparison is seriously confounded: synchronous codebooks are produced by groups of three, while asynchronous codebooks are produced by individual coders and are not consolidated, so the study does not isolate collaboration modality from group size, labor, and consensus effects.

The statistical analysis is not convincing. The paper uses unpaired t-tests and many significance claims despite very small numbers of independent coding units, dependent theme/document observations, high variance, and no correction for multiple comparisons; this risks pseudoreplication and overstated conclusions.

Several metrics are imperfect proxies for codebook quality. Best-match maximum similarity does not penalize duplicate or unmatched themes, embedding similarities are often near ceiling and heavily affected by corpus homogeneity, and intra/inter-theme similarity can reflect dataset structure or theme granularity rather than better qualitative analysis.

The correctness evaluation is underreported and only moderately reliable: 200 examples per setting may be too small for fine-grained comparisons, confidence intervals are missing, sampling appears to overweight themes rather than corpus frequency, treatment of LLM-unlabeled documents is unclear, and Krippendorff alpha is only moderate.

The experimental protocol leaves important reproducibility and validity gaps, including participant assignment, time spent, intervention counts, order effects from repeated participants always doing asynchronous work first, and differences in auxiliary information available to the systems.

The claims should be framed as exploratory. The results are mixed across datasets and systems, and some LLM prompt templates appear poorly matched to the task, which weakens confidence in broad conclusions about collaboration settings or system classes.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored NLP/HCI problem: how collaboration settings affect NLP-assisted qualitative coding outcomes, rather than evaluating tools only in isolation.
The empirical scope is commendable: three distinct interactive system paradigms, two structurally different datasets, 30 coding sessions, and 33 participants provide a useful descriptive comparison.
The evaluation is multi-dimensional, combining consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, manual post-hoc correctness checks, dataset-property analysis, and participant interviews.

The appendices include useful reproducibility material, including prompts, hyperparameters/settings, operation details, dataset statistics, and final codebooks; the stated public release of code and experimental data is a strength.
The paper surfaces practically useful observations, especially that dataset characteristics and user intervention affordances can matter as much as the nominal modeling approach.
weaknesses: The central causal claim about collaboration modality is not fully supported. Synchronous groups contain three coders producing one codebook, while asynchronous conditions appear to be single-coder outputs without consolidation, confounding modality with group size, deliberation, labor, and team reconciliation.

The statistical analysis is fragile. There are only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per condition, yet t-tests appear to treat theme/document similarities as independent observations; multiple comparisons, high variance, and repeated participant participation are not adequately handled.

The proposed quality metrics are useful proxies but incomplete. Best-match Jaccard can allow many-to-one alignments, centroid similarities are often near-saturated, and SBERT-based cohesiveness may reward surface semantic similarity rather than qualitative analytic adequacy.

The correctness evaluation is valuable but under-specified: only 200 pairs per setting are checked, agreement is moderate, confidence intervals/blinding/instructions are unclear, and post-hoc judgments may not capture whether the codebook itself is conceptually appropriate.

Generalizability is limited by the specific datasets, participant pool, and system configurations. The LLM condition uses one small model with low-to-moderate human-model agreement, so broader conclusions about LLM-based coding tools are premature.

The paper sometimes overstates descriptive trends as significant or explanatory findings. A Findings-level version would need to soften claims, use analyses that respect the experimental unit, and more directly acknowledge the async-consolidation and labor confounds.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem for NLP-assisted qualitative analysis: how collaboration conditions interact with interactive theme-discovery systems and dataset characteristics.
The empirical effort is substantial, covering three distinct system families, two datasets, 33 participants, 30 coding sessions, automatic metrics, post-hoc correctness annotation, and interviews.
The authors make a useful attempt to separate multiple notions of output quality, including consistency across codebooks, within-codebook cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and assignment correctness.

The appendix improves transparency by reporting prompts, LLM agreement/unlabeled rates, codebooks, dataset statistics, and system operation details, and the paper states that code and experimental outputs are public.
weaknesses: The central causal claim about collaboration modality is not fully supported because synchronous sessions are three-person consensus sessions while asynchronous sessions are individual sessions without later consolidation. This confounds modality with group size, deliberation, and aggregation procedure, and the studied asynchronous setting is only a partial match to real asynchronous collaboration.

The statistical analysis is not rigorous enough for the number and structure of comparisons. Theme-level similarities are nested within codebooks and participants, but the paper uses unpaired t-tests, reports many significance markers without correction, and even marks near-significance. This weakens confidence in claims about significant collaboration effects.

Several metrics are only indirect proxies for the claimed constructs. Best-match Jaccard can inflate consistency through many-to-one alignments and ignores unmatched themes/codebook-size effects; SBERT centroid similarity can be high for semantically broad or homogeneous corpora without implying thematic equivalence; the top-25% cohesiveness analysis uses system-specific confidence notions that may not be comparable.

The correctness evaluation is valuable but underreported: Figure 4 lacks exact values, uncertainty intervals, and a clear significance procedure, and the annotation rubric for deciding whether a document-theme pair is correct is not described in enough detail. The reported inter-annotator agreement is only moderate.

The LLM-based condition is a weak and somewhat unstable representative of LLM-assisted coding: Llama 3.2 3B has low human-model agreement in several sessions, nontrivial unlabeled rates, and prompts that appear inconsistently adapted. This limits conclusions about LLM-based systems broadly.

Some dataset-characteristic explanations are plausible but post hoc and occasionally internally inconsistent. For example, Table 10 appears to contradict the prose about the proportion of pairs above/below 0.3 similarity, suggesting either a table-label error or interpretation error.

The contribution is useful as an exploratory empirical study, but the evaluation framework is mostly a combination of existing similarity/cluster-quality ideas and manual spot checking; the novelty and generality are therefore moderate rather than main-conference strong.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and under-evaluated problem: how collaboration settings affect NLP-assisted qualitative coding, rather than evaluating interactive tools only in isolation.

The empirical effort is substantial: three different classes of systems, two structurally different datasets, 33 participants, 30 coding sessions, post-hoc correctness annotation, and interviews provide a richer evidence base than many prior tool papers.
The proposed evaluation dimensions of consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness are sensible and help separate different notions of codebook quality.
The paper is generally clear, well motivated, and transparent about many experimental details, including prompts, system operations, codebooks, dataset characteristics, and claimed code/data release.
weaknesses: The central causal claim about synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration is not fully supported because modality is confounded with group size and collaboration structure: synchronous sessions use three coders jointly, while asynchronous sessions appear to be individual independent coders without a consolidation phase. This makes it difficult to attribute differences specifically to synchrony rather than number of annotators, discussion, effort, or consensus formation.

The number of independent experimental units is very small, with only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system/dataset condition. The reported t-tests seem to rely on many theme/document-level quantities that are not independent, raising pseudoreplication concerns and making the statistical significance claims too strong.

Several metrics may partly evaluate properties of the embedding space or system mechanics rather than qualitative validity. In particular, SBERT-based consistency/cohesion metrics overlap with the representations used by some systems, and very high centroid similarities suggest limited discriminative value in some settings.

The correctness evaluation is useful but underspecified: it is unclear whether evaluators were blinded, how theme definitions were presented, how ambiguity was handled beyond tie-breaking, and whether the sample size is sufficient per theme/system. strengths: Addresses an important and under-studied problem: how collaboration modality affects NLP-assisted qualitative coding workflows, which is relevant to both NLP and HCI-oriented computational social science.

The empirical scope is stronger than many user studies in this area, covering three distinct tool families, two datasets with different linguistic properties, synchronous and asynchronous settings, and both quantitative and interview-based evidence.

The proposed evaluation dimensions, consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness, are sensible for theme discovery and combine document overlap, embedding-based similarity, and human post-hoc validation.

The appendices improve transparency by reporting prompts, final codebooks, theme counts, dataset diagnostics, LLM agreement statistics, and interview protocol; the paper also states that code and experimental data are publicly available.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that collaboration modality affects output quality is only partially supported. The synchronous condition uses three-person groups, while the asynchronous condition is effectively individual coding without realistic asynchronous consolidation, so modality is confounded with number of coders and deliberation structure.

The statistical testing appears underpowered and likely pseudoreplicated. With only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per tool/dataset, t-tests over theme-level or document-level quantities do not provide strong independent evidence, and there is no correction for many comparisons.

The results are mixed across tools, datasets, and metrics, but the narrative sometimes overstates broad conclusions. Several reported effects are small, inconsistent, or depend on embedding-based metrics whose validity for qualitative theme quality is not fully established.

Correctness evaluation is useful but not fully specified: the paper reports F1 scores for sampled document-theme pairs without clearly defining negatives/recall, confidence intervals, or statistical comparisons. The inter-annotator agreement is only moderate, leaving residual uncertainty about this key evidence.

Evaluation metrics may favor systems aligned with the same representation used for scoring, especially because SBERT embeddings are used in both system operation and semantic evaluation. The relationship between embedding cohesiveness and qualitative usefulness remains undertheorized.

The LLM conclusions are limited by use of a single small model, low human-model agreement in several settings, and many invalid or unlabeled outputs. This supports conclusions about this implementation more than about LLM-based qualitative coding generally.

Reproducibility is better than average for a user study, but full replication remains difficult because interactive human decisions, participant expertise, repeated participation, random seeds, and session dynamics are not described in enough detail to reproduce the main behavioral effects.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored question for NLP-assisted qualitative analysis: how collaboration modality interacts with tool design and corpus properties. This is clearly relevant to ACL/NLP, especially human-in-the-loop NLP and computational social science workflows.

The empirical scope is unusually broad for this area: three representative interactive systems, two structurally different datasets, synchronous and asynchronous settings, multiple codebooks, and a post-hoc correctness study. This makes the contribution more informative than a single-tool evaluation.

The evaluation is multidimensional, combining consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, correctness, dataset characterization, and participant interviews. This triangulation is a real strength, since no single metric can capture qualitative coding quality.

The paper is generally clear about the selected systems, datasets, coding protocol, prompts, generated codebooks, and annotation outputs, and the public release of code/data materially improves reproducibility.

The main findings are nuanced rather than one-sided: the authors show that synchronous collaboration can improve some outcomes, but effects depend strongly on system affordances and dataset characteristics.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded: synchronous conditions use groups of three, while asynchronous conditions appear to be individual codebooks rather than asynchronously produced and consolidated team codebooks. This makes it difficult to isolate collaboration modality from number of coders, aggregate expertise, and person-time.

The statistical analysis is not fully convincing. The paper reports t-tests and many significance markers, but the independent experimental units are few per cell, participants are reused, and theme/document-level measurements may induce pseudoreplication. Multiple comparisons and mixed-effects alternatives are not discussed.

Several metrics are useful but only indirect proxies for qualitative coding quality. SBERT-based cohesion and centroid similarity may reward semantic compactness rather than interpretive usefulness, and maximum theme matching can inflate consistency when many themes align to the same counterpart. Correctness sampling evaluates document-theme assignment but not codebook completeness, granularity, or theoretical adequacy.

The correctness results are mixed and sometimes undercut the stronger narrative that synchronous teamwork improves outcomes. For example, correctness shows no consistent collaboration effect across datasets/systems, so the paper should more explicitly separate evidence for cohesion/consistency from evidence for actual coding accuracy.

Generalizability remains limited: only two English political/social-media-style corpora are used, participants are NLP/CSS researchers rather than a broader range of qualitative researchers, and the LLM condition uses a single small model and selected prompting setup.

Reproducibility is helped by released artifacts, but the manuscript still lacks some operational details needed to interpret the human study rigorously, including time-on-task, participant assignment/reuse, exact interface conditions, coder training variation, and full annotation instructions for the correctness evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and under-examined problem: how collaboration modality affects NLP-assisted qualitative coding workflows, which is clearly within NLP/HCI and computational social science interests.
The empirical setup is ambitious, covering three families of interactive systems, two datasets with different properties, quantitative metrics, and follow-up interviews.
The paper makes a useful attempt to separate several notions of quality, including cross-coder consistency, within-codebook cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and post-hoc assignment correctness.
Reproducibility is partially supported by public code/data claims and appendices containing prompts, hyperparameters, theme lists, and some operational details.
weaknesses: The central claim that collaboration modality affects output quality is not adequately supported. The number of independent units is extremely small for each dataset/system/modality comparison, with only two synchronous group codebooks and three asynchronous individual codebooks, yet the paper reports broad conclusions about collaboration effects.

The statistical analysis appears vulnerable to pseudoreplication and multiple-comparison issues. Two-sample t-tests over theme/document-derived measurements do not seem to respect dependence among themes from the same codebook, coders, datasets, or systems, and no correction or hierarchical/randomization analysis is reported.

The operationalization of asynchronous collaboration is problematic. The paper defines asynchronous coding as independent coding followed by consolidation, but the experiments appear to compare individual asynchronous codebooks against synchronous group codebooks without actually modeling consolidation strategies.

Several quality metrics are only weakly validated as measures of better qualitative analysis. Embedding-based centroid and intra-theme similarities may reward semantically narrow or coarse themes, while high/low inter-theme similarity is difficult to interpret across datasets with very different global similarity distributions.

The correctness evaluation is unclear and under-specified. The figure reports F1 scores, but the text describes judging sampled assigned document-theme pairs, which would mainly estimate precision unless negatives and missed assignments are defined; the exact annotation protocol and computation are not sufficiently explained.

The LLM condition is not a convincing representative of modern LLM-based qualitative coding: it uses a small Llama 3.2 3B model, achieves low Gwet AC1 in several settings, leaves nontrivial unlabeled outputs, and may primarily measure prompt/model weakness rather than collaboration modality.

Participant assignment and study controls are insufficiently described. Some participants appear in multiple experiments, the sample is drawn from a narrow institutional population, tool/dataset/order effects are not convincingly controlled, and the qualitative interview analysis lacks methodological rigor.

The paper overclaims from mixed and sometimes contradictory results. Correctness does not show a stable collaboration effect, consistency differs by dataset/system, and some dataset-analysis tables/text contain apparent labeling or interpretation inconsistencies, yet the conclusion uses fairly strong causal language.

Each cell appears to have only two synchronous groups or three asynchronous coders, participants are sometimes reused, and many reported significance tests appear to treat nested theme/document similarities as independent. The metrics are reasonable as diagnostics but not fully validated as measures of qualitative analysis quality. The results are mixed, especially for correctness and consistency, yet the conclusions sometimes overstate synchronous collaboration benefits. The user-study component is also lightly analyzed, with limited methodological detail beyond selected themes and quotes.
